questions.question: Von Neumann architecture is based on —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) SISD.**

The classic stored-program Von Neumann machine has one instruction stream and one data stream.

questions.question: Example for zero address instructions is —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) push.**

Zero-address instructions operate on the top of a stack, so they need no explicit memory/register address.

questions.question: What is the full form of TLB?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) Translation Look-aside Buffer.**

A TLB caches recent virtual-to-physical page translations.

questions.question: What is Page Map Table?

options.text: It maps the virtual addresses to physical addresses
It maps physical addresses to virtual addresses
It maps the virtual addresses to Logical addresses

questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A.**

A page map/page table translates virtual page numbers into physical frame numbers.

questions.question: The result of `MOV AL, 65` is to store —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) 0100 0001 in AL.**

Decimal 65 is `41H`, which is binary `0100 0001`.
questions.sourceNote: Handwritten tick on the scan confirms option D; no official key was supplied.

questions.question: Which of the following is page fault?

options.text: Page fault occurs when a program accesses a page of another program
Page fault occurs when a program accesses a page in main memory
Page fault occurs when there is an error in particular page
Page fault occurs when a program accesses a page which is not present in main memory

questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D.**

A page fault traps to the OS when the referenced page is valid but not resident in main memory.

questions.question: Which of the following are the two main components of the CPU?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: C) CU and ALU.**

The control unit directs operations; the arithmetic/logic unit executes them. Registers are internal storage.

questions.question: The term that provides simultaneous data processing tasks are —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) parallel processing.**

Parallel processing executes multiple operations concurrently. Vector/array processing are more specific forms.

questions.question: A `16 × 8` organisation of memory cells can store upto —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) 128 bits.**

`16 × 8 = 128` cells/bits in the usual 16 words × 8 bits per word interpretation.

questions.question: A processor can access a memory location by 32 bits. Then find the total memory size if all memory locations are available to the processor.
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: A) 4 GB.**

A 32-bit address selects `2^32` byte-addressed locations = 4 GiB.

questions.question: Data transfer from Cache Memory to Processor is —
questions.answer:
**Correct answer per the scan annotation: B) Block by Block.**

The handwritten mark selects B. In many textbooks, cache-to-CPU transfers are word-by-word while main-memory-to-cache transfers are block-by-block, so this item is architecture-convention dependent.
questions.sourceNote: The scan’s handwritten tick selects B. A standard alternative convention would make A correct for cache-to-processor word transfers; no official key exists.

questions.question: In which of the following term the performance of cache memory is measured?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) Hit ratio.**

Hit ratio = cache hits / total accesses; miss ratio and average access time are derived from it.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT involved in the case of a memory write operation?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: D) PC.**

MAR holds the address and MDR the data; the data bus carries it. The program counter is not part of the memory write data path.

questions.question: Which of the following memory unit communicates directly with the CPU?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) Main memory.**

The CPU addresses main memory directly; auxiliary/secondary storage is reached through I/O controllers.

questions.question: A computer system supports `2^46` logical addresses and `2^11` addresses per page. How many pages can be represented in secondary memory (virtual memory address space)?
questions.answer:
**Correct answer: B) 2^35.**

The number of page frames equals the number of logical addresses divided by the page size, 2^46 / 2^11 = 2^35. The exponent is simply subtracted because both values are powers of two.
questions.sourceNote: OCR flattened `2^35` to `235`; restored from the page crop.

questions.question:
a) Draw the Von Neumann basic structure and mark all its components.
b) Draw and explain the BUS architecture of a digital computer.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Draw the Von Neumann basic structure and mark all its components.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Draw and explain the BUS architecture of a digital computer.

questions.answer:
**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 + b) 4.**

**a) Von Neumann structure (4 marks)**

```text
+---------+     +-------------------+     +----------+
|  INPUT  |---->|      MEMORY       |<--->|  OUTPUT  |
+---------+     | instructions+data |     +----------+
                +---------+---------+
                          |  single shared bus
                +---------v---------+
                |  CONTROL UNIT     |
                |  ALU  + registers |
                +-------------------+
```

The five units are **input, output, memory, ALU** and **control unit**. The defining idea is the **stored program**: instructions and data share one memory and one bus, so execution is a serial fetch-decode-execute cycle and the shared bus becomes the **von Neumann bottleneck**.

**b) Bus architecture (4 marks)**

A digital computer has three buses, each carrying one kind of information:

| Bus | Carries | Width decides |
|---|---|---|
| **Address bus** | the address of the selected word | addressable memory (`2^n` words for `n` lines) |
| **Data bus** | the actual data | word size and transfer rate |
| **Control bus** | read/write, clock, interrupt, bus grant | the protocol |

```text
CPU ---- address bus (unidirectional) ----> memory / I/O
CPU <--- data bus (bidirectional) --------> memory / I/O
CPU <--- control bus (RD, WR, M/IO) ------> memory / I/O
```

The address bus is unidirectional because only the CPU (or a DMA controller) originates addresses; the data bus is bidirectional because data flows both ways. Wider address and data buses are why a 32-bit machine can address more memory and move more per cycle than an 8-bit one.

questions.question:
a) Explain the basic instruction cycle with appropriate diagram.
b) Write the Zero address instructions to evaluate `X = (A+B) * (C+D)`.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Explain the basic instruction cycle with appropriate diagram.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Write the Zero address instructions to evaluate `X = (A+B) * (C+D)`.

questions.answer:
**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 + b) 4.**

**a) The instruction cycle (4 marks)**

```text
   FETCH --> DECODE --> FETCH OPERANDS --> EXECUTE --> STORE --> (PC update) --+
     ^                                                                        |
     +------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

1. **Fetch** — the address in the **PC** goes to the MAR, memory returns the instruction to the IR, and the PC is incremented.
2. **Decode** — the control unit interprets the opcode and identifies the operands.
3. **Fetch operands** — data comes from registers or memory into the ALU inputs.
4. **Execute** — the ALU performs the operation.
5. **Store** — the result is written back to a register or memory.

```text
PC -> MAR -> memory -> MBR -> IR ;  PC = PC + 1
IR -> decoder -> control signals -> ALU / registers
```

The cycle repeats under the clock; an interrupt between instructions inserts the ISR fetch instead.

**b) Zero-address code for `X = (A + B) * (C + D)` (4 marks)**

A **zero-address** machine keeps its operands on a stack: an operator pops its two top values, computes and pushes the result.

```text
PUSH A        stack: [A]
PUSH B        stack: [A, B]
ADD           stack: [A+B]
PUSH C        stack: [A+B, C]
PUSH D        stack: [A+B, C, D]
ADD           stack: [A+B, C+D]
MUL           stack: [(A+B)*(C+D)]
POP  X        stack: []      X = (A+B)*(C+D)
```

**Eight instructions**, and no address field at all — the stack pointer implies the operands. That is the compactness advantage of stack machines; the cost is that every expression must be evaluated in strict postfix order, with no reuse of intermediate values.

questions.question:
a) Write the difference between Minimum Mode and Maximum Mode in 8086 Microprocessor.
b) Explain with example any four addressing modes available in 8086 microprocessors.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Write the difference between Minimum Mode and Maximum Mode in 8086 Microprocessor.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Explain with example any four addressing modes available in 8086 microprocessors.

questions.answer:
**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 + b) 4.**

**a) Minimum versus maximum mode of the 8086 (4 marks)**

| Point | Minimum mode | Maximum mode |
|---|---|---|
| `MN/MX` pin | tied **high** | tied **low** |
| Bus control | produced by the **CPU** (`ALE`, `RD`, `WR`, `IO/M`) | produced by an external **8288** |
| Status | used directly | `S0-S2` decoded by the 8288 |
| Systems | single processor | multiprocessor, 8087 coprocessor, DMA |
| Extra signals | — | `LOCK`, `RQ/GT`, `QS0-QS1` |

```text
minimum: 8086 --(ALE,RD,WR,IO/M)--> memory / I/O
maximum: 8086 --(S0-S2)--> 8288 --(control)--> bus ;  other masters can arbitrate
```

Maximum mode exists so a second bus master can take over — impossible when the CPU itself drives the control lines.

**b) Four 8086 addressing modes (4 marks)**

| Mode | EA | Example | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Immediate | none (value in instruction) | `MOV AL, 25` | constants |
| Register | none (value in register) | `MOV AX, BX` | fastest operands |
| Direct | address in instruction | `MOV AL, [2000H]` | globals |
| Register indirect | address in a register | `MOV AL, [BX]` | pointers |
| Based indexed | `BX/BP + SI/DI + disp` | `MOV AL, [BX+SI+4]` | arrays, records |

```text
MOV AL, [BX+SI+4]      EA = BX + SI + 4
```

The 8086 allows only one memory operand per instruction and combines a base register (`BX`/`BP`) with an index (`SI`/`DI`), which is enough to address a 2-D array or a record field in a single instruction.

questions.question:
a) Write the different cache mapping techniques and explain it.
b) A typical computer system cache memory access time is 8 ns and its main memory access time is 80 ns. If hit ratio is 90%, what is the average memory access time?

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Write the different cache mapping techniques and explain it.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: A typical computer system cache memory access time is 8 ns and its main memory access time is 80 ns. If hit ratio is 90%, what is the average memory access time?

questions.answer:
**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 + b) 4.**

**a) Cache mapping techniques (4 marks)**

| Scheme | Placement | Address split | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Direct** | one fixed line, `j mod C` | tag, line, offset | conflict misses |
| **Fully associative** | any line | tag, offset | `C` comparators |
| **Set-associative** | any way in one set | tag, set, offset | `E` comparators, few conflicts |

```text
direct      : | tag | line | offset |
set-assoc   : | tag | set  | offset |
associative : | tag |      offset |
```

Direct mapping is cheapest and needs no replacement policy; full associativity removes conflict misses but is viable only for small caches; set-associative is the compromise used by real L1/L2 caches, because `E` candidates absorb the strided accesses that thrash a direct-mapped cache.

**b) Average memory access time (4 marks)**

Given `Tc = 8 ns`, `Tm = 80 ns`, `h = 0.9`:

```text
parallel lookup   : Tavg = h*Tc + (1-h)*Tm   = 0.9*8 + 0.1*80 = 7.2 + 8 = 15.2 ns
inclusive lookup  : Tavg = h*Tc + (1-h)*(Tc+Tm) = 7.2 + 0.1*88  = 16.0 ns
```

**Answer: 15.2 ns** on the parallel-lookup convention, 16.0 ns if a miss pays the cache time as well — state the convention. Notice that raising `Tm` from 65 ns to 80 ns lifted the average from 13.7 ns to 15.2 ns, so slow memory hurts in proportion to the miss ratio.

questions.question:
a) Write the difference between CISC & RISC Architecture.
b) Write short notes on any one: i) DMA ii) Virtual Memory.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Write the difference between CISC & RISC Architecture.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Write short notes on any one: i) DMA ii) Virtual Memory.

questions.answer:
**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 + b) 4.**

**a) CISC versus RISC (4 marks)**

| Point | CISC | RISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction set | Large, complex (300+) | Small, simple (~100) |
| Length | Variable | Fixed |
| Memory operands | allowed in ALU instructions | load/store only |
| Registers | few | many (32+) |
| Cycles per instruction | many, microcoded | ~1, pipelined |
| Control unit | microprogrammed | hardwired |
| Code density | high | lower |

```text
CISC: ADD [BX], AX       <- one instruction, memory operand, several micro-ops
RISC: LOAD R1,(R2) ; ADD R3,R1,R4 ; STORE R3,(R2)   <- three instructions, clean pipeline
```

**b) Short notes: any one (4 marks)**

**i) DMA** — a controller moves a block between memory and a device without the CPU handling each word. The CPU programs address, count and direction; the controller raises **HRQ**, receives **HLDA**, transfers by cycle stealing or burst, then interrupts on completion. It removes the per-word CPU cost of interrupt-driven I/O and sustains disk and network bandwidth.

```text
CPU: program DMA -> (work) -> interrupt
DMA: HRQ -> HLDA -> address,count,R/W -> words 1..n -> release -> IRQ
```

**ii) Virtual memory** — each process sees a large contiguous address space mapped onto physical frames and backed by disk. A reference to an absent page traps as a **page fault**; the OS loads it, evicting a victim by LRU or clock, while the **TLB** caches recent translations. It gives programs larger than memory, process isolation and simple relocation, at the cost of a translation on every access and the huge latency of a page fault.

questions.question:
a) What is biased exponent of floating-point number?
b) Discuss in detail the architecture of 8086 microprocessor along with pin configuration diagram.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: What is biased exponent of floating-point number?

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Discuss in detail the architecture of 8086 microprocessor along with pin configuration diagram.

questions.answer:
**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 2 + b) 6.**

**a) Biased exponent (2 marks)**

The exponent in an IEEE 754 floating-point number is stored **biased**: a fixed constant is added so that every stored value is non-negative. Single precision uses 8 bits with **bias 127**, so a true exponent of `-3` is stored as `124` and `+4` as `131`.

```text
stored E = true e + bias     single: bias 127    double: bias 1023
```

It lets the hardware compare magnitudes with an ordinary unsigned comparator and avoids a separate sign-and-two's-complement path for the exponent.

**b) Architecture of the 8086 (6 marks)**

```text
                 +--------------------------------------+
                 |             8086 CPU                 |
   AD0-AD15 <--->|  BIU: segment regs, IP, 6-byte queue |
   A16-A19  ---->|       address adder -> 20-bit        |
                 +------------------+-------------------+
                                    | (queue)
                 +------------------v-------------------+
                 |  EU: ALU, flags, general registers   |
                 |      AX BX CX DX SP BP SI DI         |
                 +--------------------------------------+
```

**BIU (Bus Interface Unit)** — supplies the outside world: it holds the four **segment registers** (`CS, DS, SS, ES`) and the **instruction pointer**, forms the 20-bit physical address as `segment*16 + offset`, fetches instructions into the **6-byte queue**, and performs every bus read and write.

**EU (Execution Unit)** — executes: it decodes instructions from the queue, does ALU work, sets the flags, and computes effective addresses with its general registers. It never touches the bus.

```text
physical address = segment register x 16 + offset   (20 bits from two 16-bit registers)
```

The split is a two-stage pipeline: while the EU executes, the BIU prefetches, so fetch overlaps execution. **Pins:** 40, grouped as `AD0-AD15` (multiplexed address/data), `A16-A19`, bus control (`ALE, RD, WR, M/IO, DEN, DT/R`) and handshake (`CLK, RESET, READY, INTR, NMI, HOLD, HLDA`), with **`MN/MX`** selecting minimum or maximum mode. `ALE` must latch the address off `AD0-AD15` before those pins carry data.

questions.question:
a) Explain the different groups of computers according to Flynn’s classification.
b) Write down the IEEE-754 format for single and double precision numbers.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Explain the different groups of computers according to Flynn’s classification.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Write down the IEEE-754 format for single and double precision numbers.

questions.answer:
**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 + b) 4.**

**a) Flynn's classification (4 marks)**

| Class | Instruction streams | Data streams | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SISD** | 1 | 1 | classic single-core CPU |
| **SIMD** | 1 | many | vector/SIMD units, GPUs, array processors |
| **MISD** | many | 1 | rare — systolic arrays for fault tolerance |
| **MIMD** | many | many | multicore CPUs, clusters |

```text
SIMD: one add instruction applied to 8 float pairs at once
MIMD: 4 cores, each running its own code on its own data
```

The taxonomy is coarse — it says nothing about memory organisation or interconnect — but it captures the essential step from scalar to vector to truly parallel processing.

**b) IEEE 754 single and double precision (4 marks)**

```text
single (32): | S | E (8)  |          M (23)          |
double (64): | S | E (11) |          M (52)          |
value = (-1)^S x 1.M x 2^(E-bias),  bias 127 / 1023
```

| Field | Single | Double |
|---|---|---|
| Bits | 32 | 64 |
| Exponent | 8 (bias 127) | 11 (bias 1023) |
| Fraction | 23 | 52 |
| Precision | ~7 digits | ~16 digits |

The **hidden leading 1** is not stored, so 23 stored bits give 24 significant bits. All-zero and all-one exponents are reserved for zero, subnormals, infinity and NaN.

```text
example: -6.5 -> sign 1, 6.5 = 110.1b = 1.101 x 2^2, E = 129 = 10000001
single: 1 10000001 10100000000000000000000
```

questions.question:
a) Describe the concept of Pipeline and its types.
b) Write the different types of pipeline hazards.

subparts.label: a
subparts.text: Describe the concept of Pipeline and its types.

subparts.label: b
subparts.text: Write the different types of pipeline hazards.

questions.answer:
**Mark distribution — Total 8 marks: a) 4 + b) 4.**

**a) Pipelining and its types (4 marks)**

**Pipelining** overlaps the stages of instruction execution so that several instructions are in flight at once, giving up to `k` times the throughput of a `k`-stage non-pipelined unit.

```text
cycle :  1   2   3   4   5   6
IF    : I1  I2  I3  I4  I5  I6
ID    :     I1  I2  I3  I4  I5
EX    :         I1  I2  I3  I4
MEM   :             I1  I2  I3
WB    :                 I1  I2
```

**Types:**

| Type | Idea |
|---|---|
| **Instruction pipeline** | overlap IF/ID/EX/MEM/WB of successive instructions |
| **Arithmetic pipeline** | split a long operation (float add, multiply) into stages |
| **Super-pipelining** | more, finer stages (deeper pipeline, higher clock) |
| **Superscalar** | several pipelines in parallel, issuing >1 instruction per cycle |

**b) Pipeline hazards (4 marks)**

| Hazard | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Structural** | two instructions need one resource | split I/D caches, duplicate units |
| **Data (RAW)** | operand not yet produced | forwarding, one stall for load-use, scheduling |
| **Data (WAR/WAW)** | out-of-order writes | register renaming |
| **Control** | branch target unknown | branch prediction, delayed branch, speculation |

```text
RAW: ADD R1,R2,R3 ; SUB R4,R1,R5     <- stall or forward R1
BEQ R1,R2,L      ; ...                <- mispredict costs the pipeline depth
```

The speedup is limited by the **slowest stage** (the clock must match it), by fill and drain, and by the stall rate — which is why a 5-stage design typically achieves 3-4, not 5.
